extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and performing stand-up comedians and joke-writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating strong premises for stand-up jokes: how to construct setups that create anticipation and tension (topic + condition), use persona/analogy/misdirection, and prompt a satisfying punchline. Focus is on live performance applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two dissimilar ideas converging
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the oldest definitions of a joke: 'A joke is two dissimilar ideas converging.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two different concepts and force them together in the setup so the audience anticipates how they will be reconciled; this is the foundational mechanism that creates comedic potential (historical note: Aristotle/Plato/James Beattie referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup vs. Punchline; role of the premise
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke is usually made up of a setup and a punchline. The Setup usually contains the premise. A premise is how the setup is formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The premise is what makes an audience decide if they should continue listening; it must therefore spark interest or emotion. Craft the setup so it prompts the audience to want a resolution from the punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic elements: topic + condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic elements of a premise are a topic + a condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'condition' can be a setting, situation, or point of view. Presenting a topic together with a condition creates acute anticipation for an answer, solution, or explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spark interest/emotion and create anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: A premise is what makes an audience decide if they should continue listening, so it has to spark interest or emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the premise provoke curiosity or an emotional reaction so the audience is invested in hearing the resolution; insufficient prompting leads to weak audience desire for a payoff (anti-pattern: a good setup that doesn't create enough desire for resolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter explanation through persona or state
rubrics_metrics.description: The explanation can make sense in an additional way if it is filtered through your persona, state of mind, emotional state, physical ability or disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your unique stage persona or attributes to color the premise and punchline (example given: 'I'm Irish and Native American...' leading to a persona-based punchline about AA seats). This personalization adds layers and distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt desire for resolution (use repetition and misdirection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Here's the Secret: a good premise is the audience is waiting for you to resolve the information you gave us in the setup. So you can prompt them to desire a resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics: repetition (restate facts to increase audience curiosity) and misdirection ('So you know what that means…') that forces the audience to try to fill in the blank. Example structure: SETUP (fact), REPETITION (increase tension), MISDIRECTION (prompt), PUNCH (unexpected resolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy/is-like device to impose dissimilar ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the simplest ways of imposing two dissimilar ideas is to use the device of analogy, (is-like).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements like 'Going to the gym is a lot like sex...' or 'Marriage is a lot like going to Home Depot...' posit two unlike things as the same, creating an illogical equation that makes the audience crave clarification and sets up comedic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create tension by making an illogical equation
rubrics_metrics.description: By stating this idea that can't be true at first glance, the audience is on pins and needles waiting for you to provide the solution to this outwardly ridiculous statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tension is necessary in any story to give the audience a reason to pay attention. The premise should create a need for clarification, an answer, or resolution; without tension the setup feels flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be relatable
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premises that tap into shared experiences or recognizable situations make it easier for the audience to engage and feel the tension; relatability increases payoff when the punchline resolves a common expectation in an unexpected way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antagonize (create emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Antagonize (create an emotion of excitement, frustration, confusion, fascination for the audience)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally provoke an emotional reaction — not necessarily anger, but any strong feeling — to raise stakes and attention. Emotions drive curiosity and investment in the eventual resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create imagery
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, visual language in the premise so the audience forms a mental picture; vivid imagery makes the setup more engaging and the punchline more surprising or satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create tension and a need for clarification or resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Create tension and a need for clarification, an answer, or resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft premises that leave an open question or puzzle the audience; the stronger the need for resolution, the more powerful the laugh when the punchline delivers it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep it simple; don't overthink
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't Overthink It — Some of the best jokes are the simplest jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity often works best: plainly state two dissimilar ideas, imply they are the same, then solve that statement. Avoid overcomplicating the premise; clarity helps the audience follow and react.
